fields.h1: Is the Bible Reliable? An Honest Look for Teens
fields.meta_title: Is the Bible Reliable? An Honest Answer for Teens
fields.description: You have heard the Bible was changed, contradictory, or just old myths. Here is an honest look at whether it can be trusted — at a teenager’s level.
fields.body_html:
You have probably heard it more than once: the Bible has been changed so many times that we cannot know what it originally said; it is stuffed with contradictions; and anyway it is just a pile of ancient myths dressed up as history. Those are fair things to wonder about, and you deserve a real answer rather than a slogan. The short version is this: the Bible we hold today is a remarkably well-preserved set of ancient documents, honest about the very people it holds up as heroes, and it invites your questions instead of fearing them. Trusting it still involves faith — but it is not blind faith, and the difference matters.

Let us take the objections one at a time. You are old enough for the real answers, and they are more interesting than the slogans.

“It was changed over time” — how the text reached us

The picture most people carry is a game of telephone: a message whispered down a line until it comes out garbled. If that were how the Bible got to us, we would be right to worry. But it is not.

Before the printing press, books were copied by hand. For the New Testament this went on for centuries, and the result is an enormous number of surviving copies — thousands of Greek manuscripts, thousands more in other ancient languages, plus quotations scattered through the writings of early Christians. Compare that to other famous works of the ancient world, where we often have a handful of copies made a thousand years after the original. By the ordinary standards historians use for any old document, the New Testament is the best-attested text of its age by a wide margin.

Here is why that abundance is good news rather than a problem. When you have many copies, you can lay them side by side and see exactly where a scribe slipped — a misspelled word, a skipped line, a margin note a later copyist folded in. Scholars call these differences “variants,” and there are many, precisely because there are so many manuscripts to compare. But the overwhelming majority are tiny and obvious: a name spelled two ways, a word order that changes no meaning.

The crucial point is that errors do not accumulate secretly when you have this many witnesses. If one copy drops a word, a dozen others still have it, and the disagreement is what exposes the mistake. No teaching of the Christian faith hangs on a disputed reading, and the places scholars genuinely debate are flagged right in your Bible’s footnotes — a sign of honesty, not concealment. A book hiding its seams would not print them for you.

The gap in time is short, too. Paul’s letters were circulating while eyewitnesses to Jesus were still alive and able to contradict him if he had gotten it wrong. That is not the profile of a legend that grew slowly in the dark; it is a report made in the open, while it could still be checked. So “changed over time” turns out to be half true in a way that builds confidence: yes, small variations crept in; no, we are not guessing about the result. We can reconstruct what the authors wrote with high certainty, and we can show our work.

“Full of contradictions” — hard is not the same as untrustworthy

A lot depends on a distinction people skip past. There is a difference between a passage that is hard to understand and one that is untrustworthy. They feel similar when you first hit them; they are not the same thing.

Take the accounts of Jesus’ resurrection in the four Gospels. One mentions one angel at the tomb, another two; the women arrive in a different order; the lists of who saw what do not line up perfectly. Skeptics wave this around as proof of contradiction. But think about how real eyewitness testimony works. If four friends described the same chaotic morning — the biggest shock of their lives — and matched word for word, you would suspect they had coordinated the story. The small differences are what honest, independent witnesses sound like. They agree completely on what matters — the tomb was empty, Jesus was alive — and differ on incidental details.

Many so-called contradictions dissolve the moment you ask basic questions: Is one writer summarizing while another gives detail? Are they describing two different occasions? Is one using a figure of speech? Some passages are genuinely difficult, and mature Christians have wrestled with them for centuries. But “I do not yet see how these fit together” is a very different claim from “this has been proven false.” The Bereans in Acts 17:11 are praised for exactly this posture: they welcomed the message eagerly, then examined the Scriptures to check whether it was so. Examining is not the enemy of faith; lazy dismissal is. So when you hit a hard passage, hold the question open and investigate it. Do not let a difficulty you have not looked into pose as a verdict you have reached.

A book that tells on its own heroes

Here is something that may surprise you. If people were inventing a religion and writing propaganda for it, they would make their founders look good — that is how invented stories work. The Bible does the opposite, relentlessly.

  • David, the model king, commits adultery and then arranges a man’s death to cover it up (2 Samuel 11) — and the Bible records his broken confession in Psalm 51 for everyone to read forever.
  • Peter, the leading apostle, denies three times that he even knows Jesus and weeps bitterly (Matthew 26:74–75). His own preaching became part of the Gospel record, including his shame.
  • Abraham lies to save his own skin. Moses loses his temper. The disciples squabble about who is greatest and abandon Jesus when it counts most.

Historians have a name for this: embarrassing details tend to be true, because nobody invents material that makes their own side look bad. The Bible is soaked in such details. It reads like people telling the truth about themselves even when it humiliates them, because they cared more about what happened than about looking good. A book this honest about human failure takes the real world seriously — the world where people you admire let you down and you let yourself down. Myths make their heroes shine; the Bible lets its heroes bleed. That is a strong reason to take it as truth rather than flattering legend.

“Just old myths” — and the science-textbook mix-up

Part of what people mean by “myths” is that the Bible sometimes speaks about the world in ways that do not sound like a science class. It opens with a soaring account of creation in Genesis 1:1 and following, so people conclude it must be primitive and false. But this confuses two kinds of writing doing two different jobs. A science textbook tells you the mechanism — how gravity works, how cells divide. The Bible tells you what a textbook never can: who made the world, why you are here, what has gone wrong with the human heart, and what God has done about it. Asking the Bible to work as a chemistry manual is like being angry that a love letter has no wiring diagram.

Notice how Genesis opens. It does not argue for God’s existence or explain the mechanics of creation; it announces that in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth, then turns at once to the questions it cares about — the dignity of human beings, the goodness of the world, our relationship with our Maker. It answers different questions than a science class, and the two are not in a cage match. As for “myth” in the sense of made-up legend, the New Testament writers rejected that flatly. Peter says they did not follow cleverly devised myths but were eyewitnesses of what they reported (2 Peter 1:16). Luke opens his Gospel (Luke 1:1–4) by explaining that he carefully investigated everything, drawing on eyewitnesses, so his reader could have certainty. These are not people spinning fables around a campfire.

How Jesus and the apostles treated Scripture

If you take Jesus seriously at all, his own attitude toward the Bible is hard to ignore. He did not handle Scripture as a bundle of nice old stories; he treated it as the word of God — true, authoritative, binding on him. Tempted in the wilderness, he answered every attack by quoting it, saying that people live not on bread alone but on every word from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4). He said Scripture cannot be broken, and that not the smallest letter would pass away until everything was accomplished (Matthew 5:18). He told people to search the Scriptures because they testified about him (John 5:39).

The apostles followed him. Paul wrote that all Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, correcting, and training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16), and that the things written in the past were written to teach us and give us hope (Romans 15:4). Isaiah 40:8 puts it memorably: the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God endures forever. You do not have to accept that on the spot, but see that trusting the Bible is not a fringe move Christians invented recently to win arguments. It is the settled posture of Jesus himself and of the people who walked with him and died rather than take it back.

Faith is involved — and that is not a cheat

Let me be candid, because you can smell a dodge a mile away. None of this adds up to a mathematical proof that leaves you no choice. Faith is involved. But do not let anyone convince you that faith means believing with no reasons. Biblical faith is trust placed on good grounds — the way you trust a friend who has proven honest, or sit in a chair you have not personally stress-tested. You have reasons, then you commit beyond what you can prove with total certainty, because that is how trust in a person always works.

The Bible does not ask you to switch your brain off. Remember Thomas, who refused to believe Jesus had risen until he saw for himself. Jesus did not scold him for wanting evidence — he showed up and told him to put his finger in the wounds and stop doubting (John 20:27). The invitation was to look. And 1 Peter 3:15 tells Christians to always be ready to give a reason for the hope in them, with gentleness and respect — a faith commanded to give reasons is not afraid of them. The Bible is also honest about the one thing it says we cannot fix ourselves: that the human heart is deceitful (Jeremiah 17:9), yours and mine included, which is exactly why we need a word from outside ourselves rather than our own shifting feelings about what is true.

Read it for yourself

Here is the most important thing in this whole article. Almost everyone who tells you the Bible is unreliable is telling you what they heard about the Bible. Very few have actually read it with an open mind. You do not have to live secondhand on other people’s summaries, whether they come from skeptics or from Christians.

Pick up one of the Gospels — start with Mark, it is short and fast — and read it straight through, watching what Jesus actually says and does, with your questions switched on. Notice whether it reads like a fairy tale or like testimony, and whether it flatters its characters or tells the truth about them. Bring your doubts along; the Bereans did, and so did Thomas, and neither was turned away. You may find, as many honest skeptics have, that the book is stranger, tougher, and more truthful than anyone warned you — and that it can bear the full weight of your hardest questions. Whether it can bear the weight of your whole life is something only reading it, and coming to know the God it points to, can finally show you. But you will never know if you only ever hear about it from a distance. So read it firsthand. Start today.
